title: El Niño's long shadow over fuel demand | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Wood Mackenzie models a very strong 2026-27 El Nino as a multi-year income shock that cuts global gasoline, diesel and jet demand, benign in aggregate but severe by region and sector. Road transport bears most of the loss, North America the largest volume hit, and Latin America and Africa the steepest proportional hit.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie expects a very strong El Nino peaking in northern winter 2026-27 to reduce global demand for gasoline, diesel and jet fuel, with the aggregate figure looking contained while regional and sectoral impacts are not.
insights.speaker: Gordon  McManus
insights.so_what: Headline oil-demand numbers may understate localized demand destruction; positioning should look below the global aggregate.
insights.quote: At the aggregate level, the figure looks like it is contained. At the regional and sectoral level, it does not.
insights.locator: A very strong El Niño, peaking

insights.claim: The model averages GDP-per-capita losses from the three strongest El Nino events on record (1982-83, 1997-98, 2015-16) and converts each country's projected income loss into reduced fuel use via income elasticities adjusted for product type and region.
insights.speaker: Gordon  McManus
insights.so_what: The demand estimate rests on historical analogues and elasticity assumptions, so it is sensitive to whether this event matches past ones.
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie modelled the demand impact

insights.claim: For fuel markets the critical variable is the redistribution of rainfall and heat (drought in some regions, floods in others), not the temperature shift itself.
insights.speaker: Gordon  McManus
insights.so_what: Track regional precipitation outcomes rather than global temperature headlines when assessing energy demand risk.
insights.quote: that redistribution is the critical variable, not the temperature shift itself
insights.locator: 1. How income loss, not weather, drives

insights.claim: Agriculture, hydropower, freight and electricity demand absorb the El Nino disruption; these channels cut GDP and household income, and lower income translates directly into lower fuel consumption.
insights.speaker: Gordon  McManus
insights.so_what: Fuel demand is hit second-order via incomes, so the lag extends beyond the weather event.

insights.claim: The weather event ends but the income shortfall persists, so the demand effect extends well past the weather event that triggers it.
insights.speaker: Gordon  McManus
insights.so_what: Demand-loss timing is longer than a seasonal view implies, which matters for forward curves and refining margins.
insights.quote: The weather event ends. The income shortfall does not.

insights.claim: Road transport carries the heaviest burden of the El Nino fuel-demand loss, with gasoline and diesel accounting for much of the total and aviation most of the remainder.
insights.speaker: Gordon  McManus
insights.so_what: Downside concentrates in road fuels, the core of refined product demand, rather than being spread evenly.
insights.quote: Road transport carries the heaviest burden, with gasoline and diesel accounting for much of the overall loss.

insights.claim: Jet fuel is the most income-sensitive product per barrel in the analysis.
insights.speaker: Gordon  McManus
insights.so_what: Jet demand is the highest-beta product to an income shock, so airline and jet-crack exposure is more vulnerable.
insights.quote: jet fuel the most income-sensitive product per barrel

insights.claim: Each year after the event, affected economies fall further behind the growth path they would otherwise have followed, making this a compounding multi-year income drag rather than a seasonal disruption.
insights.speaker: Gordon  McManus
insights.so_what: Cumulative demand loss builds over years, which is relevant to long-dated supply and capex assumptions.
insights.quote: Lost growth compounds. This is a multi-year income drag, not a seasonal disruption.
insights.locator: The trajectory of the loss matters

insights.claim: North America records the largest volume loss from the El Nino scenario, with the United States making up the majority of the regional total, reflecting market scale rather than depth of climate exposure.
insights.speaker: Gordon  McManus
insights.so_what: US income response is the swing factor for global volume impact.
insights.quote: Its prominence reflects the scale of the market, not the depth of its climate exposure.

insights.claim: Latin America and Africa carry the steepest proportional losses because they include economies reliant on rain-fed agriculture and hydropower, which shortens the distance between weather shock and income loss.
insights.speaker: Gordon  McManus
insights.so_what: Emerging-market fuel demand and related credit and FX exposures are more vulnerable than OECD volumes suggest.
insights.quote: shortening the distance between weather shock and income loss

insights.claim: Asia Pacific shows country-level dynamics moving in different directions, with hydropower, back-up generation, aviation and other factors shaping liquid fuel impacts.
insights.speaker: Gordon  McManus
insights.so_what: Asia may contain offsetting effects, such as hydropower shortfalls raising back-up generation fuel use, so net impact is ambiguous.

themes.theme: Drivers of final impact and investor implications

insights.claim: The final intensity of the 2026-27 El Nino will determine the income shock in the most exposed economies; US economic performance through 2028 matters most for volume, and the pace of Andean market recovery shapes the Latin American share and depth of the loss curve.
insights.speaker: Gordon  McManus
insights.so_what: Key variables to monitor: El Nino intensity, US growth through 2028, and Andean recovery.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie says the income channel is the mechanism sustaining the fuel-demand effect, and that this carries direct implications for capital allocation by energy companies, commodity traders and infrastructure investors with exposure to affected regions.
insights.speaker: Gordon  McManus
insights.so_what: Capital allocation and supply assumptions in exposed regions may need revisiting; details are in the full report.
insights.quote: the income channel is the mechanism that sustains it
